narrative: A young man from Aleppo, once accepted to a university in Latakia, saw his studies interrupted by the war and left for Turkey in 2013, where he worked as a hairdresser and sent money home to his mother and sister, who lived on the dangerous edge of the regime-rebel divide in Aleppo. He decided to leave for Europe with a friend he had met years earlier at the national exam. They found their smuggler on Facebook and paid $1,000 each for a boat from Turkey to Greece, setting off in daylight in a rubber dinghy with 43 people packed so tightly he lost feeling in his legs. Not far from the shore of the Greek island of Agathonissi, the Algerian steering the boat stabbed it with a knife so the approaching Greek Coast Guard could not force them back to Turkey; the boat sank and everyone panicked, but all made it to the rocky shore. On Agathonissi they spent a night in a police cell, then slept outside, and were fed only once in two and a half days before being sent to Samos, where they waited a week for papers. They took a ferry to Athens and a train north, then crossed into Macedonia, one of the most difficult countries on the route. Their first attempt, in the mountainous west, ended after two days of walking in rain and mud when police stopped them at Bitola; his attempt to bribe the officers only angered them, and he was handcuffed while other officers beat an older man with batons before trucking them back to the Greek border with a warning. A second attempt also ended in capture. On their third try they joined a group of about 70 leaving at 4 a.m., walking silently through a wheat field with women and children in the middle and men carrying sticks, and crossed the country in nearly 30 hours. In Serbia, at a train station, they joined hands and danced with other refugees to the music of two buskers - a rare moment of joy. In Belgrade he ran out of money and nearly stayed behind to find work, but a friend wired him $800. From the border town of Kanjiza the group of eight took a bus, then hiked along train tracks through fields of paprika toward Hungary, hiding in shrubs until dark, turning off their phones for fear of being tracked, some clutching box cutters against thieves. They crossed into Hungary undetected and paid $140 each for a ride to Budapest, where the group split. He and his friend paid a man $1,345 to drive them to Germany, and were dropped on the road just across the Austrian border; they walked an hour to Passau and bought tickets to Hamburg before a police officer spotted them at the station. The officer gave them an apple and a banana and explained they should apply for asylum, and they stayed overnight. In the morning another officer woke them gently, apologizing. They had traveled more than 1,500 miles. He settled at an asylum center in Freyung, in Bavaria, and was anxious to get his mother and sister out of Aleppo, afraid that the Islamic State would soon seize the city.
